lessons.title: Pharma, Utilities, and Telecom: Non-Discretionary and Regulated Earnings

body.text: Medicines, electricity, and a mobile connection are things people cannot easily go without. But demand is only half the story. Each of these sectors is protected by a different wall, and each wall has its own crack: the regulator for utilities, the USFDA and US pricing for pharma, and competitors for telecom.

children.text: The last lesson covered consumer staples, the purest defensives. This lesson covers the other sectors most Indian investors and fund managers lean on when they want to reduce economic risk. They do reduce it. What they add instead are risks that have nothing to do with GDP, and you need to see those clearly before you treat any of them as a safe haven.

children.text: Utilities: When the Regulator Sets Your Return

markDefs.definition: A pricing method where the regulator allows a company to recover its approved costs, such as depreciation, interest, and operating expenses, plus a fixed return on the equity it has invested.

children.text: Power Grid's inter-state transmission assets are largely regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) on a

. The company is paid for keeping its lines available, not for how much electricity flows through them. So when industrial demand slows, its revenue barely notices. What drives its earnings is how much capital it has invested in completed assets, and the return the regulator allows on that capital.

body.title: Calculate the Regulated Return
body.prompt: A transmission line costs ₹10,000 crore and is funded 70% by debt and 30% by equity, the standard normative ratio used in CERC tariffs. If the allowed return on equity is 15.5%, how much return on equity, in ₹ crore, does the tariff build in each year?
body.explanation: Equity = 30% × ₹10,000 crore = ₹3,000 crore. Return = 15.5% × ₹3,000 crore = ₹465 crore a year. This return does not depend on GDP growth or electricity consumption, only on the asset being available and the regulator's allowed rate. Interest on the ₹7,000 crore of debt is recovered separately through the tariff.

body.title: Power Grid Consolidated Net Profit, FY15 to FY26 (₹ crore)

children.text: Two things stand out. First, profit rose every year from FY15 to FY22, compounding at about 18.8% a year, straight through the FY20 slowdown and the pandemic. Second, from FY22 to FY26 profit went essentially flat, around ₹15,400 crore to ₹16,800 crore. Nothing cyclical happened. Growth slowed because Power Grid's investment in new regulated assets had slowed. For a regulated utility, the growth driver is capex, not the economy.

body.text: Power Grid's borrowings rose from about ₹96,000 crore in FY15 to about ₹1.48 lakh crore in FY26. In Chapter 2, debt was what turned Tata Steel's downturns into losses. Here it does not, because interest on approved debt is recovered through the regulated tariff. Debt is dangerous when revenue can fall while interest cannot. When revenue is contracted to cover interest, the same debt is far less risky.

children.text: The cracks in the utility wall are regulatory, not economic. Allowed returns are reset for each multi-year tariff period, and CERC's regulations for 2024 to 2029 set a lower return on equity for new transmission assets than for older ones. More new transmission projects are also awarded through competitive bidding, where returns depend on how aggressively the company bid. And for power generators, which sell to state distribution companies, delayed payments from financially weak discoms can tie up cash for long periods.

A diabetes or heart patient does not stop taking medicine because GDP slowed. That makes pharma demand genuinely non-discretionary. But most large Indian pharma companies earn a big share of revenue from exporting generic medicines to the US, and that business carries shocks that have nothing to do with India's economy.

body.caption: Sun Pharma consolidated, ₹ crore (source: Screener.in annual figures)

children.text: Read this table the way Chapter 1 taught. In FY18, operating profit fell 44.3% and net profit fell 67.6%, as US generic price erosion and regulatory issues hit, while India's economy was doing fine. That is a company-specific shock, not a cyclical one. After FY18, operating profit grew every single year through FY26, including the pandemic. The weak net profit in FY21 and FY22 came from large one-off charges, visible on Screener.in as negative other income of about ₹3,500 crore in each year, not from weak operations.

body.title: How drug price controls work in India

children.text: Medicines listed in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) are subject to ceiling prices under the Drug Price Control Order, administered by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA). Companies cannot sell these medicines above the ceiling. Ceiling prices are revised each year in line with the Wholesale Price Index, which means that when input costs rise faster than the WPI, margins on controlled products get squeezed. For investors, the practical question is what share of a company's domestic sales comes from price-controlled medicines.

markDefs.definition: Average Revenue Per User: total revenue from subscribers divided by the number of subscribers, usually shown per month. It is the key pricing metric for telecom operators.

children.text: Chapter 1 traced how the Jio price war and consolidation moved telecom along the spectrum. Here are the numbers behind that story. Telecom has very high fixed costs, towers, fibre, and spectrum payments, so it carries heavy operating leverage. That means
matters enormously. When a price war cuts ARPU, the loss drops straight to profit. When tariffs rise, almost all of the increase does too.

stats.label: Airtel sales, FY16 to FY19
stats.context: ₹96,532 crore to ₹80,780 crore during the price war

children.text: Airtel's operating profit multiplied 4.52 times while sales grew 2.61 times, which is operating leverage working in the shareholder's favour after tariffs rose. Today telecom behaves much more defensively, because three private players have little incentive to restart a price war and customers keep paying through slowdowns. But its protection is industry structure, and industry structure can change. That is why telecom belongs in the quasi-defensive band rather than next to HUL.

body.title: The Telecom Pricing Metric
body.textWithBlank: Because most of a telecom operator's costs are fixed, changes in ___, its average revenue per user, flow almost directly into operating profit.
body.explanation: With towers, fibre, and spectrum costs largely fixed, a tariff increase that lifts ARPU adds revenue with little extra cost, while a price war that cuts ARPU removes revenue without reducing costs.

body.title: Match the Risk
body.question: An economist forecasts a sharp slowdown in Indian industrial activity next year. Which of these companies' earnings are LEAST likely to be directly affected by that slowdown itself?
options: A regulated power transmission company paid for line availability
body.explanation: A transmission company paid on a cost-plus basis for keeping lines available earns its regulated return regardless of how much power industry consumes. The other three depend directly on industrial and construction activity. The transmission company's key risks are regulatory, such as future changes to allowed returns, not economic.

body.title: The Pharma Fund as a Recession Hedge
body.scenario: Priya, a mutual fund investor, expects India's economy to slow. She plans to move most of her equity SIP into a pharma and healthcare sectoral fund, reasoning that people always need medicines. Looking at the fund's factsheet, she sees its top holdings are large Indian pharma companies, several of which earn 30% to 50% of revenue from the US.
body.prompt: Is a pharma fund the defensive hedge Priya thinks it is? What should she consider?
body.modelAnswer: Partly. Domestic medicine demand is non-discretionary, so an Indian slowdown should not hurt these companies much. But Priya is swapping economic risk for different risks, not removing risk. With large US exposure, the fund's earnings depend on US generic pricing, USFDA inspection outcomes, and the rupee-dollar exchange rate, none of which relate to India's economy. Sun Pharma's FY18, when profit fell 67.6% while India was growing, shows these shocks can be severe. Sectoral funds are also concentrated: a regulatory event affecting several holdings hits the whole fund. Moving most of her SIP into one sector breaks diversification. A more balanced approach is to hold defensive exposure across several sectors, such as staples, pharma, and utilities, sized as part of a diversified portfolio.

body.label: Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC)
body.description: Tariff regulations, including allowed returns on equity, that determine earnings for regulated power generation and transmission companies.

points: Utilities, pharma, and telecom all serve non-discretionary demand, but each is protected by a different mechanism with its own risks
Regulated transmission earns a cost-plus return on invested equity; its growth depends on capex and its main risk is regulatory change
Debt that is recovered through contracted or regulated tariffs is far less dangerous than debt in a business whose revenue can fall
Pharma demand is steady, but US generic price erosion, USFDA actions, and domestic price controls create company-specific shocks unrelated to GDP
Telecom has necessity demand and heavy operating leverage; its defensiveness depends on industry structure staying rational
Sectoral funds in these areas swap economic risk for concentrated sector risk, so size them within a diversified portfolio

This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security or fund.
